title: Midterm Review
description: One question from each of the 21 sample-test types: 18 multiple-choice questions, a two-part memory trace, and two C implementations.

source.title: CSCI 2122 Practice Questions for Mid-Term
source.attribution: Dalhousie University Faculty of Computer Science
source.note: Original questions and choices are transcribed from the supplied PDF. Answer keys, explanations, clarifications, and new variants were created for this review; they are not an official instructor answer key.

assumptions: Use C17, ASCII, 8-bit bytes, and 32-bit int/unsigned int unless an item specifies a different bit-width model.
Bit and nibble indices start at zero at the least significant end. 1u means an unsigned int constant with value 1.
Assume standard declarations are available, all stated objects are valid, and no concurrent changes occur.
Originals with missing context or typos carry visible clarifications. Fixed-width wrapping exercises are explicitly distinguished from C integer promotions.
For exam-style practice, follow the sample’s no-calculator, no-notes instruction. Answers are shown after submission.

groups.title: Data, context, and interpretation
groups.competency: Distinguish stored bits from the information needed to interpret their meaning.
review: Identify the data and the missing interpretation rule separately.
Review instruction sets, file formats, type information, and signedness.
Explain why the same bits can represent different values or instructions.

groups.title: Memory hierarchy
groups.competency: Rank storage levels by typical access latency and distinguish latency from capacity.
review: Recall registers → cache → RAM → secondary storage.
Order L1, L2, and L3 within a conventional cache hierarchy.
Distinguish fastest-to-slowest from slowest-to-fastest; access time from capacity.

groups.title: Pointers and formatted output
groups.competency: Trace aliases and dereferences, then match printf conversions to argument types.
review: Track an address separately from the value at that address.
Match %d to int and %p to a void pointer.
Distinguish a compile-time constraint violation from undefined runtime behavior.

groups.title: Valid array and pointer statements
groups.competency: Decide which assignments and pointer operations satisfy C type and object rules.
review: Arrays cannot be assigned as whole objects.
Array expressions usually convert to pointers to their first elements.
Review const, pointer-to-array types, and one-past pointers.

groups.title: Hexadecimal to binary
groups.competency: Translate every hexadecimal digit into four bits without changing byte order.
review: Memorize the four-bit patterns for hexadecimal digits 0–F.
Keep leading zeros for a specified width.
Distinguish a number’s written binary representation from byte order in memory.

groups.title: String input and buffer capacity
groups.competency: Account for the null terminator and scanf field width when finding safe input lengths.
review: A C string needs one byte beyond its visible characters.
A %s field width excludes the terminating null byte.
Width-limited input can leave the rest of an overlong token unread.

groups.title: Nibble extraction
groups.competency: Trace a shift-and-mask helper and identify the selected hexadecimal digit.
review: Number nibbles from zero at the least significant end.
Each hexadecimal digit spans four bits; isolate it with 0xF.
Use unsigned operands or explicitly state signed conversion/shift assumptions.

groups.title: Sign, parity, and byte order
groups.competency: Infer sign and parity from a fixed-width two’s-complement bit pattern.
review: The highest value bit determines the sign in two’s complement.
The lowest value bit determines odd/even parity.
Little endian changes byte placement, not the value’s sign or parity.

groups.title: Alternative bit-string interpretations
groups.competency: Compare unsigned, sign-magnitude, and two’s-complement interpretations of the same bits.
review: Unsigned uses every bit as a positive weight.
Sign-magnitude separates the sign bit and magnitude.
For negative two’s complement, subtract 2^width from the unsigned value.

groups.title: Sign extension
groups.competency: Widen a two’s-complement bit pattern while preserving its signed value.
review: Repeat the original sign bit in the added high positions.
Positive values extend with zeros; negative values extend with ones.
Check the decimal value before and after widening.

groups.title: Bits discarded by shifts
groups.competency: Determine when shifting right and then left loses information.
review: Inspect the low k bits discarded by a right shift of k.
For nonnegative values, unchanged means divisible by 2^k.
Distinguish a fixed-width bit exercise from promoted signed C expressions.

groups.title: Cross-nibble field extraction
groups.competency: Extract a masked field that may span hexadecimal digit boundaries.
review: Identify the rightmost source bit of the field.
Shift that bit to position zero, then apply the width mask.
Work nibble by nibble, especially for shifts not aligned to a whole byte.

groups.title: Two’s-complement decoding
groups.competency: Convert a fixed-width negative hexadecimal pattern to signed decimal.
review: Determine the intended width before deciding the sign.
Compute unsigned value minus 2^width when the top bit is set.
Check minimum, maximum, minus one, and leading-zero cases.

groups.title: Negation and integer promotion
groups.competency: Separate fixed-width wrapping negation from actual C evaluation after promotions.
review: Zero equals its own negation.
The minimum signed pattern is also self-negating in a wrapping fixed-width model.
An 8-bit signed char promotes to int before unary minus on the stated C machine.

groups.title: Signed and unsigned comparison
groups.competency: Apply promotions and the usual arithmetic conversions before comparing values.
review: The U suffix changes the type of an integer constant.
A negative int converted to unsigned int becomes a large nonnegative value.
An unsigned char can promote to int; an unsigned int remains unsigned.

groups.title: Narrowing and widening conversions
groups.competency: Trace low-byte conversion and subsequent sign or zero extension under stated assumptions.
review: Unsigned narrowing is reduction modulo 2^width.
Signed out-of-range conversion is implementation-defined in C17.
Plain char signedness must be specified before predicting a negative result.

groups.title: Packed bit-array indexing
groups.competency: Split a global bit index into byte index, local bit position, and a one-bit mask.
review: For eight-bit bytes, byte index is i / 8 and local index is i % 8.
For nonnegative i, i >> 3 and i & 7 implement those operations.
Distinguish a set mask from a complemented clear mask and from the byte index.

groups.title: Recognizing linked-list behavior
groups.competency: Infer a traversal’s contract from its initialization, comparison, update, and return.
review: Trace what happens for an empty list, head, middle node, and tail.
Compare node identity separately from equality of stored values.
Check whether the return value is a Boolean, count, index, or pointer.

groups.title: Tracing memory and pointer updates
groups.competency: Record array contents and pointer destinations after each statement.
review: Pointer addition moves by elements, whose addresses differ by sizeof(element).
Dereferencing changes the object at the address; pointer reassignment changes the address.
Distinguish *p++, (*p)++, p[i], and a one-past pointer.

groups.title: Writing string traversal functions
groups.competency: Implement a terminating scan and compute the requested string length or closely related count.
review: Stop at the first null character and do not count it.
Initialize counters and advance exactly once per examined character.
Test empty strings, offsets, bounds, and embedded nulls as the contract requires.

groups.title: Writing byte-oriented memory functions
groups.competency: Implement exact byte writes with correct bounds and pointer return semantics.
review: Convert void * to a character pointer before byte-wise access.
Write precisely the requested range, preserving bytes outside it.
Test zero size, interior ranges, byte conversion, and the required return pointer.

questions.question: Given an object file compiled on some other system and you are asked: What does the code do? What statement best describes the situation?
options: This is not possible as there is no data.
This is not possible as there is no data and no context.
This is possible because there is data and context.
This is not possible as there is no context.
questions.explanation: Under the stated missing-context assumption, D is the intended answer: the file provides data, but its interpretation is unknown. As written, the PDF is under-specified: many real object formats identify their architecture and can be analyzed. This is a conditional, independently derived key.
questions.note: For this original, assume the target instruction set and object format are unknown and cannot be identified from metadata. “Compiled elsewhere” alone would not establish that interpretation is impossible.

questions.question: You receive raw machine-code bytes with no file header and no known target instruction set. What best describes your ability to decode the instructions?
options: Neither stored data nor decoding context is present.
Data is present; the decoding context is missing.
Context is present; the stored data is missing.
Both data and decoding context are present.
questions.explanation: The bytes are the data. Instruction-set knowledge supplies the rules that map those bytes to instructions.

questions.question: The same 8-bit pattern is read as either an unsigned integer or an ASCII character. What determines which interpretation is appropriate?
options: The number of ones in the stored byte.
The physical address of the byte alone.
The type or encoding expected by the surrounding program.
The time at which the byte was written.
questions.explanation: The bit pattern has no unique meaning by itself. The consumer’s type or encoding supplies the interpretation.

questions.question: An object file declares its target architecture and format in a recognized header, and a matching disassembler is available. Which conclusion is justified?
options: Its instructions can be decoded using that context.
Its instructions cannot be decoded because it was compiled elsewhere.
Its exact original C source must be uniquely recoverable.
Its exact original variable names must all be recoverable.
questions.explanation: Recognized metadata and a matching decoder supply context. Decoding instructions does not guarantee recovery of exact source or names.

questions.question: You know a file contains 16-bit integers but do not know the byte order. What information is still missing?
options: How successive bytes contribute to each integer’s value.
Whether the file contains any stored data.
How many bits are stored in each integer.
How many distinct 16-bit patterns are possible.
questions.explanation: Width is known, but byte order is needed to assign high and low significance to each byte.

questions.question: A debugger displays the same bytes once as a floating-point value and once as an integer. Which statement explains the differing values?
options: Different interpretation rules are applied to the same data.
The integer view always exposes the one true meaning.
The bytes must have changed between the two views.
The floating-point view always exposes the one true meaning.
questions.explanation: A debugger can reinterpret unchanged storage through different type rules. Neither view is inherently the correct application meaning.

questions.question: A protocol says one byte is an unsigned count. The byte is 0xFF. Which statement best describes this situation?
options: The data is available but every interpretation rule is missing.
The interpretation rule is available but the data is missing.
Neither the data nor an interpretation rule is available.
Both the data and its interpretation rule are available.
questions.explanation: The protocol supplies unsigned-count context and the byte supplies the data, so the value is 255.

questions.question: A bit sequence is given with no width, signedness, or encoding. What can be stated with certainty?
options: The supplied bit sequence itself is known.
Its machine instruction is uniquely known.
Its text character is uniquely known.
Its signed decimal value is uniquely known.
questions.explanation: The literal bits are observable. Their intended numeric, text, or instruction meaning requires additional context.

questions.question: A program stores 0x41 in memory. One component expects ASCII text and another expects an unsigned byte. Which statement is valid?
options: The components may read A and 65 from the same bits.
The unsigned interpretation changes the stored bits to A.
The components must read the same displayed text.
The ASCII interpretation changes the stored bits to 65.
questions.explanation: In ASCII, the code for A is 65, which is 0x41. Different displays need not imply a storage change.

questions.question: A file format is documented but the file’s payload bytes are unavailable. What best describes the missing information?
options: Interpretation context is known, but the data to interpret is missing.
The data is known, but all interpretation context is missing.
Both the payload data and its context are known.
The format description uniquely determines every payload byte.
questions.explanation: A format describes how to interpret content; it does not supply the actual content of a particular file.

questions.question: Two instruction sets assign different instructions to the same byte pattern. What information selects the correct instruction decoder?
options: The target instruction set used to encode the bytes.
The compiler optimization level alone, regardless of the target.
The byte order alone, regardless of the instruction set.
The original source language, regardless of the target.
questions.explanation: The target instruction set selects the decoding rule. Source language, byte order, or optimization level alone cannot identify that rule.

questions.explanation: I and II are type-correct assignments to a pointer variable. III and IV attempt to assign to an array, which is not a modifiable lvalue. An automatic uninitialized ptr would make actually evaluating I unsafe; this question is about assignment validity.

questions.explanation: A pointer is assignable; a whole array is not. Both a + 2 and &a[0] have type int *.

questions.question: What is the binary representation of the 32 bit hex value 0xcafedead?
questions.explanation: Each hexadecimal digit contributes four bits: C A F E D E A D becomes 1100 1010 1111 1110 1101 1110 1010 1101. The last original option also has an inconsistent group width.

questions.question: What is the binary representation of the 32-bit hexadecimal value 0xA17C03E9?
questions.explanation: Translate the digits in their written order: 1010 0001 0111 1100 0000 0011 1110 1001. Endianness does not reverse a number’s written representation.

questions.question: The following function is passed the arguments 0xcafedead and 3. The return value is:
questions.explanation: i * 4 is 12. Shifting right by 12 places puts the fourth nibble from the right (D) into the low position, and 0xF isolates it. Hexadecimal D is decimal 13.
questions.note: Assume 32-bit two’s-complement int, conversion of the argument preserves its low 32 bits, and signed right shift is arithmetic. These are machine assumptions, not universal C17 guarantees.

questions.question: The function is called as mystery(0xA17C03E9u, 0). What value is returned?
questions.explanation: The shift is 0 × 4 = 0 bits. Nibble index 0, counting from zero on the right, is 9; masking with 0xF returns decimal 9.

questions.question: The function is called as mystery(0xA17C03E9u, 7). What value is returned?
questions.explanation: The shift is 7 × 4 = 28 bits. Nibble index 7, counting from zero on the right, is A; masking with 0xF returns decimal 10.

questions.question: The function is called as mystery(0x08F2B640u, 3). What value is returned?
questions.explanation: The shift is 3 × 4 = 12 bits. Nibble index 3, counting from zero on the right, is B; masking with 0xF returns decimal 11.

questions.question: The function is called as mystery(0xDEAD102Fu, 4). What value is returned?
questions.explanation: The shift is 4 × 4 = 16 bits. Nibble index 4, counting from zero on the right, is D; masking with 0xF returns decimal 13.

questions.question: The function is called as mystery(0x7F0081C3u, 2). What value is returned?
questions.explanation: The shift is 2 × 4 = 8 bits. Nibble index 2, counting from zero on the right, is 1; masking with 0xF returns decimal 1.

questions.question: The function is called as mystery(0x80000001u, 6). What value is returned?
questions.explanation: The shift is 6 × 4 = 24 bits. Nibble index 6, counting from zero on the right, is 0; masking with 0xF returns decimal 0.
